title: Implement event messaging with Azure Managed Redis

questions.q: Which command subscribes to every channel that starts with ai: ?

options.text: SUBSCRIBE `ai:*`
options.why: SUBSCRIBE takes exact channel names.

options.text: PUBLISH `ai:*`
options.why: PUBLISH sends a message.

options.text: XREADGROUP `ai:*`
options.why: XREADGROUP reads Streams.

options.text: PSUBSCRIBE `ai:*`
options.why: Correct. PSUBSCRIBE subscribes with pattern matching.

questions.hint: Pattern subscriptions have their own command, which starts with P.
questions.explain: SUBSCRIBE for named channels, PSUBSCRIBE for patterns.

questions.q: When a new embedding model is deployed, every running API instance must clear its cached embeddings immediately. Which Redis feature fits?

options.text: A hash with one field per API instance
options.why: A hash doesn't notify anyone.

options.text: Pub/sub: publish an invalidation message
options.why: Correct. Every active subscriber receives the broadcast at once.

options.text: An atomic counter that instances poll
options.why: Polling adds delay; pub/sub pushes immediately.

options.text: A Stream with a consumer group of API instances
options.why: A consumer group gives each message to just one instance.

questions.hint: Every instance must hear the same signal right away.
questions.explain: Broadcasting cache invalidation is a core pub/sub use case.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A sentiment analyzer subscribes to `conversations:new` and restarts for 30 seconds during a deployment.

rows.text: Messages published during those 30 seconds are delivered when it reconnects.
rows.why: Pub/sub has no persistence; offline subscribers miss messages.

rows.text: The publisher is told the message wasn't received.
rows.why: Pub/sub is fire-and-forget; publishers don't know who received messages.

rows.text: Other subscribers that stayed connected receive those messages.
rows.why: Redis delivers to all active subscribers.

questions.hint: Pub/sub only reaches subscribers that are connected at that moment.
questions.explain: At-most-once, no persistence, fire-and-forget.

questions.q: A subscriber processes model-prediction events more slowly than they're published, and its memory keeps growing. Which pub/sub limitation is this?

options.text: Channel naming rules
options.why: Channel names don't affect delivery rate.

options.text: Pattern subscriptions
options.why: Patterns don't cause this.

options.text: No backpressure handling
options.why: Correct. Redis keeps delivering even if subscribers can't keep up.

options.text: At-most-once delivery
options.why: At-most-once is about missed messages, not slow consumers.

questions.hint: Redis keeps sending even when a subscriber can't keep up.
questions.explain: Without backpressure, slow subscribers can run into memory issues or message loss.

questions.q: A billing service must charge for every completed AI request, even if the billing service is briefly offline. Should it consume events through Redis pub/sub?

options.text: Yes, if the channel name includes the user id
options.why: Channel names don't add durability.

options.text: Yes, if it uses PSUBSCRIBE instead of SUBSCRIBE
options.why: Pattern subscriptions don't add durability.

options.text: Yes: Redis stores pub/sub messages until they're acknowledged
options.why: Pub/sub messages aren't stored or acknowledged.

options.text: No: pub/sub has no durability, so offline periods lose events
options.why: Correct. Use something durable (such as Streams) when messages must not be lost.

questions.hint: Billing can't miss events. Does pub/sub keep messages for offline consumers?
questions.explain: Pub/sub suits real-time notifications, not scenarios that need durability or replay.

questions.q: A service publishes "prediction ready" events, and the team asks how the publisher will know whether any subscriber processed each one. What does Learn say about pub/sub?

options.text: Redis retries delivery until every subscriber confirms
options.why: Pub/sub has no retries. Messages are delivered once to connected subscribers.

options.text: Messages are stored until a subscriber calls XACK
options.why: XACK belongs to Streams, not pub/sub.

options.text: It's fire-and-forget: publishers don't know whether any subscriber received the message
options.why: Correct. Pub/sub decouples publishers from subscribers, so there's no delivery confirmation.

options.text: PUBLISH returns an acknowledgment from each subscriber after processing
options.why: Subscribers don't acknowledge processing back to the publisher in pub/sub.

questions.hint: Pub/sub trades guarantees for speed and loose coupling.
questions.explain: Pub/sub characteristics: at-most-once delivery, no persistence, fire-and-forget (publishers don't know if anyone received the message), and high throughput.

questions.q: Browser clients should see AI predictions the moment the backend publishes them to a Redis channel. Which pattern does Learn show?

options.text: A backend subscriber that forwards each message over WebSocket connections
options.why: Correct. Combining pub/sub with WebSockets pushes real-time updates to browsers.

options.text: Browsers poll a Stream with XRANGE every second
options.why: Polling adds latency and load. The pattern is to push over WebSockets.

options.text: Browsers connect to Redis directly and run SUBSCRIBE
options.why: Browsers don't connect to Redis. A backend service bridges the two.

options.text: The backend writes each prediction to a cookie
options.why: Cookies travel with requests. They can't push new data to the browser.

questions.hint: Something on the server has to hold an open connection to each browser.
questions.explain: Learn's example combines pub/sub with WebSocket connections: a backend subscriber receives channel messages and pushes them to connected browser clients.

questions.q: Status channels are named ml:models:resnet:status, ml:models:bert:status and so on. One monitoring service must receive the status of every model, including ones added later. Which subscription fits?

options.text: PSUBSCRIBE `ml:models:*`:status
options.why: Correct. A pattern subscription matches every channel with that shape, including new ones.

options.text: SUBSCRIBE ml:models:resnet:status ml:models:bert:status
options.why: This lists today's channels and misses models added later.

options.text: SUBSCRIBE `ml:models:*`:status
options.why: SUBSCRIBE takes exact channel names. Patterns need PSUBSCRIBE.

options.text: XREADGROUP on a stream named ml:models
options.why: That reads a Stream, not pub/sub channels.

questions.hint: You need a wildcard, and wildcards need a particular command.
questions.explain: Channels are strings. PSUBSCRIBE subscribes with patterns such as `ai:conversations:*` or `ml:models:*`:status, so new matching channels are included.

questions.q: Which command marks a Stream task as completed by a consumer?

options.text: XREADGROUP
options.why: XREADGROUP reads tasks.

options.text: XADD
options.why: XADD adds tasks.

options.text: XINFO
options.why: XINFO reports metrics.

options.text: XACK
options.why: Correct. XACK acknowledges completion.

questions.hint: Streams have three commands: add, read in a group, acknowledge.
questions.explain: XADD → XREADGROUP → XACK.

questions.q: An upload endpoint must return immediately while documents are analyzed later, and no document may be lost if a worker crashes. What should the endpoint do?

options.text: Process the document inside the request
options.why: That blocks the API.

options.text: Store the job in a string with a 60-second TTL
options.why: An expiring string can disappear before processing.

options.text: XADD the job to a Stream and return a job id
options.why: Correct. Streams keep tasks until acknowledged and let workers process at their own pace.

options.text: PUBLISH the job to a channel and return
options.why: Pub/sub would lose jobs if no worker is listening.

questions.hint: Return quickly and keep the job safe from worker crashes.
questions.explain: Streams give durable async queues for long AI operations.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. Workers read from a Stream with a consumer group, and one worker crashes after reading a task but before XACK.

rows.text: The task stays in the pending list.
XPENDING can show tasks that have been pending too long.
The task is deleted when the worker's connection drops.
XACK was already sent automatically when the worker read the task.
rows.why: The worker must call XACK after processing; it crashed before that.

questions.hint: An unacknowledged task stays pending, and you can inspect it.
questions.explain: Pending lists and XCLAIM make Stream processing self-healing.

questions.q: A queue Stream processes millions of tasks a day and Redis memory keeps climbing, although every task is acknowledged. Why?

options.text: Pending tasks are duplicated on each read
options.why: Reading doesn't duplicate entries.

options.text: Consumer groups disable eviction
options.why: Learn doesn't say this.

options.text: Acknowledged entries stay until trimmed
options.why: Correct. Tasks don't auto-expire; trim with maxlen on XADD or XTRIM.

options.text: XACK copies each task into a second stream
options.why: XACK doesn't copy tasks.

questions.hint: Acknowledging doesn't delete. Trim the stream.
questions.explain: Plan trimming upfront: xadd(…, maxlen=10000, approximate=True) or periodic XTRIM.

questions.q: Put the steps of a reliable Stream worker in order.
steps: Create the consumer group once (ignore the error if it exists)
questions.hint: Create the group, read, process, acknowledge.
questions.explain: Unacknowledged tasks remain pending for retry.

questions.q: A pipeline needs microsecond-level notifications that a model finished loading, and losing one notification is acceptable. Should you use a Stream?

options.text: No: pub/sub is faster and loss is acceptable
options.why: Correct. Streams add a few milliseconds for persistence and acks; pub/sub fits low-latency, loss-tolerant notifications.

options.text: No: Streams can't hold more than one message
options.why: Streams hold many entries.

options.text: Yes: pub/sub can't send to more than one subscriber
options.why: Pub/sub broadcasts to all subscribers.

options.text: Yes: Streams have lower latency than pub/sub in every case
options.why: Streams are slightly slower than pub/sub.

questions.hint: Does this need durability, or speed?
questions.explain: Choose Streams for reliability, pub/sub for the lowest latency.

questions.q: A new analytics service is added next month and must process every inference request already queued in a Stream, from the beginning. Which Streams benefit makes this possible?

options.text: Streams broadcast each entry to subscribers in real time
options.why: That describes pub/sub, which doesn't keep history.

options.text: Streams delete entries as soon as they're read
options.why: Entries stay in the Stream until trimmed.

options.text: Streams keep history, so new services can catch up
options.why: Correct. You can query, replay for debugging, or let new services catch up on historical data.

options.text: Streams keep entries for subscribers connected at the time
options.why: That's pub/sub's limitation. Streams persist entries.

questions.hint: Unlike pub/sub, a Stream remembers what was added to it.
questions.explain: Streams benefits: tasks survive crashes, automatic retry via pending entries, built-in work distribution with consumer groups, processing history (replay and catch-up), and simple async patterns.

questions.q: An inference queue Stream should keep roughly the last 10,000 entries and drop older ones as new tasks arrive, without a separate cleanup job. How can the producer do this?

options.text: Set a 10,000-second TTL on each entry
options.why: Stream entries don't get individual TTLs.

options.text: Call XADD with maxlen=10000 and approximate=True
options.why: Correct. XADD can trim the stream as it adds, keeping about the last 10,000 entries.

options.text: Call XACK with count=10000
options.why: XACK acknowledges entries. It doesn't trim the stream.

options.text: Use PUBLISH instead of XADD
options.why: That moves to pub/sub, which loses durability.

questions.hint: The add command itself can cap the stream's length.
questions.explain: Acknowledged entries stay until trimmed. Cap a stream with XADD …, maxlen=N, approximate=True, or trim it separately with XTRIM.

questions.q: Three worker instances subscribe to the same pub/sub channel for inference requests. What happens when one request is published?

options.text: All three workers receive and process it
options.why: Correct. Pub/sub duplicates messages to every subscriber, tripling the cost.

options.text: Redis queues it until a worker is idle
options.why: Pub/sub doesn't queue messages.

options.text: One worker gets it, chosen round-robin
options.why: Pub/sub doesn't load-balance.

options.text: The first worker to acknowledge it keeps it
options.why: Pub/sub has no acknowledgments.

questions.hint: Pub/sub copies each message to every subscriber.
questions.explain: Use Stream consumer groups to distribute work.

questions.q: A worker restarts and should first finish tasks it had already received but not acknowledged. Which read ID should it pass to XREADGROUP?

options.why: * isn't used to read pending messages.
> returns only new messages never delivered to any consumer.
Correct. An ID such as 0 reads this consumer's pending messages.
Learn doesn't use $ for this.

questions.hint: New messages use one special ID. Your own unacknowledged ones start from the beginning of your pending list.
questions.explain: > for new work; 0 to re-read your own pending tasks.

questions.q: Match each scenario to the Redis approach.

items.text: Feature flag changed; every service must reload its config
items.why: All instances need the same update.

items.text: Each document summary job must run on exactly one GPU worker
items.why: Consumer groups give each message to one consumer.

items.text: Queue a large document for processing and tell dashboards it arrived
items.why: Queue the work in a Stream and broadcast the notification.

questions.hint: Broadcast to everyone, or hand each job to exactly one worker.
questions.explain: Broadcast vs coordinate: choose by whether everyone or exactly one should act.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A Stream consumer group scales from two workers to five.

rows.text: The new workers start receiving tasks without code changes.
rows.why: New workers in the group automatically share the work.

rows.text: Each task is now delivered to all five workers.
rows.why: Each message goes to exactly one consumer in the group.

rows.text: Each worker gets a smaller share of the total workload.

questions.hint: Consumer groups split work, and more members means smaller shares.
questions.explain: Consumer groups scale horizontally by simply adding consumers.

questions.q: A monitoring service should reassign tasks that have been pending for more than five minutes because their worker crashed. Which commands does it use?

options.text: PUBLISH to announce them, then SUBSCRIBE to retry
options.why: Pub/sub can't reassign Stream tasks.

options.text: XADD a copy of each task, then XACK the original
options.why: Duplicating tasks risks double processing.

options.text: XTRIM the stream so stuck tasks are removed
options.why: Trimming deletes entries rather than recovering them.

options.text: XPENDING to find them, XCLAIM to reassign
options.why: Correct. XPENDING finds stuck tasks; XCLAIM moves them to a healthy worker.

questions.hint: One command lists entries nobody acknowledged. Another transfers them to a different consumer.
questions.explain: XPENDING + XCLAIM keep tasks from being lost when workers crash.

questions.q: When a user finishes an AI interaction, the analytics, billing and recommendation services must each react in their own way. Losing an event for one service is acceptable. Which approach does Learn describe for notifying them?

options.text: Publish one event to a channel that all three services subscribe to
options.why: Correct. Pub/sub suits notifying heterogeneous services that each process the same event.

options.text: Add the event to one Stream read by a single consumer group of all three services
options.why: A single consumer group gives each entry to one consumer, so only one service would get each event.

options.text: Write the event to a Redis List that all three pop from
options.why: Popping removes the item, so only one service would get it.

options.text: Call each service's API in turn from the web request
options.why: That couples the request to every service. Pub/sub decouples them.

questions.hint: All three need the same event. Should it be copied or distributed?
questions.explain: Use pub/sub when all services must react to the same event (cache invalidation, configuration updates, monitoring, notifying heterogeneous services). Use Stream consumer groups to distribute work so each task runs once.

questions.q: Three GPU workers each subscribe to the channel ai:inference:requests. Costs tripled, and results are inconsistent. What should the team change?

options.text: Add a fourth worker to spread the load
options.why: With pub/sub, a fourth worker would also process every request.

options.text: Have the workers use PSUBSCRIBE instead of SUBSCRIBE
options.why: Pattern subscriptions still broadcast every message to every subscriber.

options.text: Move the requests to a Stream that the workers read through one consumer group
options.why: Correct. Consumer groups deliver each entry to only one worker, which distributes the load.

options.text: Publish each request three times, once per worker
options.why: That multiplies the duplication.

questions.hint: Pub/sub duplicates messages. What distributes them instead?
questions.explain: Pub/sub broadcasts, so every worker processes every request. Stream consumer groups give each message to exactly one consumer, enabling horizontal scaling without duplicate work.
